opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real constraint, but probably a smaller one than people intuitively expect. The reason management looks hard to automate is that there's no big, clean dataset of "here's a manager's decision, here's the outcome, here's the counterfactual." Feedback loops are long and noisy. If you reorganize a team, you might not know for a year whether that was a good call, and even then it's confounded by a hundred other things. So you can't just do supervised learning on management the way you can on, say, code completion, where you get tons of examples and fast verification.

But I'd push back on the idea that this makes management uniquely protected. First, a lot of what managers actually do is decomposable into things where we do have lots of data: communication, reading people, synthesizing information, writing plans, prioritizing tasks. Models trained on enormous amounts of human text already absorb a great deal of implicit knowledge about how organizations work, how people respond to incentives, what tends to go wrong. Second, humans themselves don't learn management from a big labeled dataset. A new manager learns from a fairly small number of experiences plus general world knowledge and social intuition. If AI systems get to the point where they have the sample efficiency and generality of humans, then the data scarcity hurts them about as much as it hurts us, which is to say, not fatally.

Where I think it does matter is timing. Domains with abundant data and fast feedback will get automated first, and things like high-level management, strategy, long-horizon judgment, will probably lag, because you need models that can learn from sparse feedback and act coherently over long time horizons. That's a capability we don't fully have yet. Once AI systems are deployed widely inside firms, they'll also start generating exactly the kind of data that's missing now: lots of decisions, lots of outcomes, at a scale no human manager ever experiences. An AI that has effectively "managed" thousands of projects could end up with far more relevant experience than any human executive.

So my view is that limited data delays AI outperforming human managers but doesn't block it. It's more a statement about the order in which things get automated than about whether they will be.

r001.rationale: The response says data scarcity need not fatally prevent AI from outperforming managers, but does not connect that prospect to sufficiently poor human management or explicitly say AI could do so with relatively little training data.

r002.rationale: It explains that management outcomes are delayed, noisy, and confounded, making it hard to tell whether a decision was good—clearly communicating the difficulty of evaluating management with a good benchmark.

r003.rationale: The response discusses deploying AI inside firms, but does not identify persuading people to work for an AI manager as a prerequisite for assessing its performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important and underappreciated points when people think about how fast AI is going to automate the economy. The basic observation is that the things AI has gotten really good at are the things where we have enormous amounts of data about what good performance looks like. Code is the obvious example. There's a huge corpus of code on the internet, you can verify whether it runs, whether it passes tests, and so on. Math is similar. You can check the answer.

Management is almost the opposite of that. The amount of data that exists about what a manager actually does day to day, and crucially about what the good decisions were versus the bad ones, is tiny by comparison. Most of it isn't written down at all. It's conversations, it's judgment calls about people, it's deciding what not to do. And even when there's some record of it, the feedback loop is incredibly noisy and delayed. You make a hiring decision and you find out whether it was good two years later, and even then it's confounded by a hundred other things. So you can't just train on it the way you train on code.

Now, I don't think that means AI can never outperform human managers. I think the question is more about the timeline and the mechanism. There are a few ways it could still happen. One is that a lot of the relevant skills transfer from other domains. If you have a model that's very good at reasoning, very good at modeling other people from all the text it's read, a lot of that general capability might carry over even without a lot of direct management data. Humans do this too. Nobody becomes a manager by being trained on millions of management episodes. They get maybe a few years of experience and they generalize from everything else they know.

The second mechanism is that once you deploy these systems in real organizations, you start generating the data. So you get a kind of bootstrapping where the initial systems are mediocre managers, but you get a lot of feedback relatively quickly because the AI can run many more instances in parallel than any human could. That's a pretty big structural advantage. A human manager gets maybe thirty or forty years of career to learn from their mistakes. An AI system deployed across thousands of companies could compress that enormously, at least in principle.

But I'd be cautious about the second one, because the feedback is still slow in calendar time. You can parallelize across companies but you can't really parallelize across time. If the outcomes you care about take years to show up, having a thousand copies doesn't help you learn faster about those long-horizon things. So I'd expect AI to get good at the parts of management with faster feedback first, like coordinating tasks, keeping track of what everyone is doing, communicating clearly, and lag on the parts that are about long-term judgment.

The third thing I'd say is that part of what looks like a data problem might actually be a measurement problem. We don't have great data on management partly because we don't actually know how to evaluate managers. If that's the bottleneck, then it's not clear AI solves it, because the problem isn't lack of training signal, it's that we don't agree on what the target is.

So overall my view is that this is a real reason to expect management and similar high-level roles to be automated later than things like software engineering, maybe quite a bit later. But I don't think it's a fundamental barrier. It's more that the path runs through general capability improvements and gradual deployment rather than through the kind of direct scaling on domain data that got us here with code. And if you believe the general capabilities keep improving, you should probably expect it to eventually get there regardless. It's just not the first thing that falls.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may generalize from other capabilities and eventually outperform managers despite limited direct data, but it does not state that sufficiently poor human management could make this possible with relatively little training data.

r002.rationale: It says we do not know how to evaluate managers well and do not agree on the target, identifying evaluation as a measurement problem.

r003.rationale: The response discusses deploying AI in organizations to generate feedback, but does not say that persuading people to work for an AI manager is a prerequisite for assessing its performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes the question more uncertain. With something like programming, you have a lot of examples of code, and you can often check whether the output works. With management, a lot of the relevant information is private or never written down, and it’s much harder to tell whether a decision was good. If a team succeeds, was that because of the manager, or would it have succeeded anyway?

That could make it harder to train an AI to be a good manager, especially through imitation. But I wouldn’t infer from that that AI can’t outperform human managers. Humans also learn to manage with fairly limited experience. They draw on more general abilities to understand situations, communicate, and make decisions. An AI might be able to do something similar.

So I’d distinguish between a shortage of management data making progress slower and it imposing a ceiling on performance. I think there’s a reasonable case for the first, but the second is much less clear. And the lack of clean feedback makes it harder for us to establish when an AI actually is better.

r001.rationale: The response says AI might draw on general abilities and could outperform human managers, but it does not say that sufficiently poor human management would enable this with relatively little training data.

r002.rationale: It says management decisions are hard to evaluate and that the lack of clean feedback makes it harder to establish whether AI is better, conveying the difficulty of benchmarking performance.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify persuading people to work for an AI manager as a prerequisite for assessing its performance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes the timeline more uncertain, because management is an area where the feedback is quite poor. If a manager makes a decision and the company does better six months later, it’s hard to know how much of that was due to the decision and how much was due to other things. So you don’t have the kind of clear training signal you get from, say, writing code and running tests.

But I wouldn’t conclude from that that AI can’t outperform human managers. Humans are learning from this same limited, noisy feedback, and an AI could potentially draw on experience across many more organizations than any individual person. The question is how much of the relevant context it can actually access. A lot of what a manager knows isn’t in a document; it comes from conversations, relationships, and understanding what people are likely to do.

So I’d expect AI to become useful for particular management tasks before we have strong evidence that it can replace the whole role. And demonstrating that it’s a better manager could take substantially longer than demonstrating that it’s a better programmer, simply because the outcomes are slower and harder to measure.
